criteria.name: literal_chars_in_filters
criteria.description: Do the submitted tests call Match or MatchUntil with filters in which `*` or `>` sits inside a longer token (such as `a*`, `*a`, `**`, `>b` or `a>`), and check that such a token matches only a stored token with exactly the same bytes, so that, for example, a filter `KV.a*` does not report stored subjects like `KV.apple`?
criteria.reasoning: The tests include filters such as "KV.a*" (in the corpus filters list) against stored subjects KV.a, KV.apple, KV.avocado, KV.banana. They also use filters with tokens like a*, *a, **, a>, >b, etc. checkLiteralFilter uses a token-level model where a non-exact `*` or `>` token matches only identical bytes, and it asserts the reported set exactly equals the expected set, with an error on any unexpected subject and on count mismatches. So KV.apple being reported for KV.a* would fail. Both Match and MatchUntil are called (stop<0 uses Match, otherwise MatchUntil).

criteria.name: literal_chars_in_stored_subjects
criteria.description: Do the submitted tests insert subjects that have `*` or `>` inside a longer token (such as `a*`, `*a`, `**`, `>b` or `a>`) into the tree and check which filters match those stored subjects?
criteria.reasoning: The tests insert subjects containing `*` or `>` inside longer tokens (a*, *a, **, a>, >b, >>, a*b, a>b, *>) in corpus and small-tree tests, then check many filters against a token-level model via Match/MatchUntil, comparing the callback results with the model and with the stored contents. Filters include the literal subjects, so stored literal subjects are checked for which filters match them.

criteria.name: real_and_literal_wildcards_mixed
criteria.description: Do the submitted tests use at least one filter that combines a real wildcard (a token that is exactly `*`, or a last token that is exactly `>`) with a `*` or `>` inside another, longer token of the same filter, and check the subjects it matches?
criteria.reasoning: The corpus and tests include filters mixing real wildcards with literal ones in longer tokens (e.g. "a*.>", "*.a*", "a*.*.end", "**.*", ">b.*"). These are verified against a token-level model via checkLiteralFilter, which asserts the matching subjects.

criteria.name: long_subjects_and_filters
criteria.description: Do the submitted tests check Match or MatchUntil results for subjects and filters of any length and any number of tokens, that is, not only for short subjects and filters with few tokens but also for longer ones with more tokens?
criteria.reasoning: The corpus includes subjects and filters with many tokens. For n in 31, 64, 257, 1024, it builds prefixes of n bytes ("p" repeated) and deep subjects of n tokens ("x." repeated n times). Filters include deep+"**.*", deep+"*.end" and deep+">b.>", with up to about 1026 tokens. These are checked through checkLiteralFilter against a token-level model, using Match and MatchUntil with several stop values, and the assertions would fail if results were wrong. Short ones are covered too, so both short and long subjects and filters are tested.

criteria.name: each_match_reported_once
criteria.description: Do the submitted tests check that Match reports every matching stored subject exactly once and nothing else (a missing, an extra or a repeated report makes the check fail), with checks that do not depend on the order of the callback calls? Any sound way of checking this counts, for example comparing the reported subjects with the expected ones as a collection, or checking each reported subject as it arrives against the expected matches and the subjects already reported and then checking the number of calls.
criteria.reasoning: checkLiteralFilter computes the expected match count from a model. In each callback it checks that the subject is in contents, matches the filter, and has not been seen before. A duplicate, extra or wrong subject sets a problem. The seen map is then compared with the expected count, so a missing report fails. The checks use a map and a count, so they don't depend on callback order. With stop = -1 or 0 it covers Match and full MatchUntil, and the unit checks run across many tree shapes. This meets the criterion.

criteria.name: match_until_stops
criteria.description: Do the submitted tests check MatchUntil's stop: once the callback returns false there is no further callback call and MatchUntil returns false, while MatchUntil returns true when the callback never returns false?
criteria.reasoning: checkLiteralFilter calls MatchUntil with stop values 0 (never false) and 2 (returns false when len(seen) reaches stop). It checks that completed equals !(stop>0 && want>=stop), so it expects false when stopped and true when it never stops. It also checks len(seen) == min(want, stop). If a callback were called after returning false, len(seen) would exceed stop, because the callback records every call and the count would be wrong. Since seen is keyed by subject and duplicates are flagged, an extra call would add to seen or set an error. So the stop is verified. The reference checks every k up to the match count. This submission checks stops 1 and 2 in several tests, and stop 2 in the main shape test. Together these cover the criterion adequately.

criteria.name: callback_receives_stored_value
criteria.description: Do the submitted tests check that the value pointer the callback receives is the stored value itself, for example by comparing it with the pointer Find returns for the reported subject, or by writing through it and reading the stored value back?
criteria.reasoning: The tests check that the callback's value pointer is the stored value. checkLiteralFilter calls st.Find on each reported subject and flags a failure if p != value. This helper runs in nearly every test. TestLiteralWildcardCallbackWrites also compares the pointer with Find's result and writes through it (*v += 10). It then reads the values back by running Match and MatchUntil and comparing against the model. That covers both approaches the criterion names.

criteria.name: results_after_updates
criteria.description: Do the submitted tests check Match or MatchUntil results again after the tree was changed by Delete or Empty (and, where relevant, by later Insert calls), against what the tree holds at that point?
criteria.reasoning: TestLiteralWildcardTreeShapes builds the tree, then deletes about two thirds of the subjects and re-inserts the rest with new values. It then calls check(filters), which runs Match and MatchUntil against the model map. It then calls Empty() and clears the model, and checks again. Last, it re-inserts every subject and checks again. checkLiteralFilter compares callbacks and counts against the current contents, including values, Find pointers, and stop behavior. This covers Match and MatchUntil after Delete, Empty, and later Insert calls. The checks are less fine-grained than the reference's per-change checks, but they meet the criterion.

criteria.name: overlapping_calls
criteria.description: Do the submitted tests run Match or MatchUntil concurrently from several goroutines, and also call Match or MatchUntil from inside a callback of a running Match or MatchUntil on the same tree, checking the results of those calls?
criteria.reasoning: TestLiteralWildcardReentrantAndConcurrent does both. Nested: inside the callback of an outer Match or MatchUntil on trees[0], it calls checkLiteralFilter on the same tree. That helper runs Match or MatchUntil with stop values -1, 0 and 1, and the results are checked against the model. Concurrent: 4 goroutines run checkLiteralFilter, which calls Match or MatchUntil, over shared trees (k = (i+w)%2), and each result is checked. The outer subject is copied and verified, and the outer visit count is also checked.

guard.reasoning: The submission is Go test code. Its comments describe test behavior, such as not assuming callback order and copying slices. None of them address an evaluator or say how the work should be scored.
